title: Capstone Walkthrough: Returns Graph
objective: After this lesson you will be able to assemble the full returns-resolution graph (state, nodes, routers, gates, checkpointing, tools) from the course's pieces, evaluate it on a gold set with per-segment diffs, and present it as traced runs plus a findings memo — ready for the final assessment and your capstone project.
why: Nine lessons of pieces; one lesson of assembly. The capstone walkthrough performs the complete build once — state design, contracted nodes, tested routers, approval gates, checkpointed threads, tool boundaries, gold evaluation — so your project repeats a demonstrated shape instead of inventing one. Assembly is itself the final skill.

blocks.text: The build order (gates at every arrow)

Assemble in dependency order, verifying each arrow: (1) **state + routing table** on paper with routing tests first (Ch.2+4); (2) **nodes with contracts** reusing Prompt 101 pack pieces (Ch.3); (3) **edges + interrupt + checkpointer**, demonstrating approve/edit/skip (Ch.5–6); (4) **tools** for order lookup with validated args (Ch.7); (5) **gold set + baseline** with per-segment scores (Ch.9); (6) **one iteration** with measured delta. Each stage runs before the next begins — integration surprises surface early, not at demo time.

blocks.caption: Manifest-first assembly: declare the whole, then build arrow by arrow

blocks.text: Three traced runs (the demo that proves)

Present three runs with full traces: **happy** (late parcel → shipping → draft → log, 4 steps, no gates); **edge** (vague multi-issue → human → clarified → decide → draft); **interrupt** ($500 refund → approval gate → edited amount → revalidated → executed). Each run shows trace + key state + timing: the happy proves flow, the edge proves routing, the interrupt proves governance. Demos without traces are theater; with traces, evidence.

Close with the memo: baseline scores (overall + per-segment), the one iterated fix with its delta, router coverage numbers, gate health (approval rate, queue latency design), checkpoint cost measurement, and deferred list (fraud subgraph next, trigram-equivalent prompt work). Measured, cited, improvable — the artifact that survives contact with stakeholders.

blocks.title: Audit the manifest
blocks.note: Run it: expect four PASS lines then 'manifest sound'. Structural audits like this catch dangling edges and untested paths before runtime does — manifest-first means machine-checkable architecture.

items: Assemble in dependency order with verification per arrow: state/routes → nodes → edges/gates → tools → eval → iterate
Present three traced runs (happy/edge/interrupt) with state + timing — evidence, not theater
Memo: baselines, per-segment diffs, gate health, checkpoint costs, deferred list

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the manifest audit and confirm soundness. (b) Break it deliberately (point one router at a nonexistent node) and record the audit output. (c) Draft your capstone manifest (same shape, your domain's nodes/routers/gates) with one entry per lesson Ch.1–9 represented.
hints: Baseline sound first; broken manifest must print FAIL + BROKEN — the audit's value proven by catching.
Your manifest needs: state list, node list, ≥2 routers with tested branches, ≥1 gate with 3 paths, persistence line, eval line.
Map entries to lessons explicitly (state→Ch.2, routers→Ch.4, gates→Ch.6…): coverage thinking for architecture.
exercise.solution:
// (a) 4× PASS + sound. (b) dangling target → FAIL + BROKEN (audit works).
// (c) domain manifest with lesson-mapped entries (coverage thinking).
exercise.why: Manifest auditing makes architecture machine-checkable; deliberate breakage proves the checker's worth; lesson-mapped manifests prove course coverage. Assembly verified three ways.
exercise.code: // Manifest-audit pattern: structural invariants as runnable checks.

quiz.q: Assembly order for the capstone graph?
options: State + routing tests → contracted nodes → edges/gates/checkpointing → tools → gold eval → one iteration — dependencies first, verified per arrow
quiz.explain: Dependency order with per-arrow verification surfaces integration surprises early. State and routing tests precede everything they govern.

quiz.q: Which three runs prove the graph, and what does each prove?
options: Happy (flow), edge (routing), interrupt (governance) — with traces, state, timing each
quiz.explain: Coverage by run-kind: flow, routing-under-uncertainty, human governance. Traces make each run evidence rather than theater.

quiz.q: Manifest audit flags a router target missing from nodes. Meaning?
options: Dangling edge: runtime crash/loop on that branch — architecture checked before execution
quiz.explain: Structural audits catch what tests miss when coverage is partial: unroutable branches. Machine-checkable architecture beats hopeful assembly.

summary: Manifest, dependency-ordered assembly, three traced runs, findings memo with per-segment truth. The course's nine lessons become one operating graph — assessment next, capstone after.
next: Course complete: take the 12-question final assessment (70% to pass), then ship the Returns-Resolution Graph capstone — and step into the CrewAI team course.
